terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Build the fitting bench here and run it, and watch which repairs end when a part does not fit.

tasks.title: Open a repair with its parts, and leave nothing behind
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/fitting.cpp`, `openWithParts` takes a ticket as an `int`, an item as a reference to a `const std::string` and the parts as a reference to a `const std::vector<std::string>`, and gives back a `std::unique_ptr<Repair>`. It makes a new repair, fits each part to it with `fitPart` in order, and gives back the owner of the repair. When a part does not fit, `fitPart` throws `std::runtime_error`, and the exception goes on to the caller.

Today, each time a part does not fit, a repair is left in memory that nothing can delete. Mend `openWithParts` so nothing is left behind, whether a part fits or not. Check builds this task with a `Repair` of its own that counts every repair made and ended, and a `fitPart` of its own that throws for parts it chooses. It counts what is left, and catches what comes out.
nextSteps: Run the program and read which repairs end, and which never do.
Find the line that can throw, and the line after it that was meant to hand the repair to an owner.
Make the owner on the same line that makes the repair, before anything can throw.
Give that owner back at the end.
hints: When fitPart throws, every line after it is skipped, the one that makes the unique_ptr included. The plain pointer is a local and ends; the repair it points at does not.
A std::unique_ptr made at once, with std::make_unique, is a local too: when the exception leaves the function, it ends and deletes the repair.
The shape is `std::unique_ptr<Repair> repair = std::make_unique<Repair>(ticket, item);`, the loop with `fitPart(*repair, part);`, then `return repair;`.

videos.title: Exceptions and cleanup that always runs

tasks.title: Borrow a tool, and always put it back
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, write a class called `Borrowed`. Its constructor takes the drawer as a reference to a `std::map<std::string, int>`, which says how many of each tool are in it, and a tool's name as a reference to a `const std::string`. It takes one of that tool out of the drawer. When the drawer has none of it, the constructor throws a `std::runtime_error` whose `what()` names the tool, and changes nothing. Its destructor puts the tool back. A `Borrowed` cannot be copied, nor copied over another: a copy would put the tool back a second time.

Check makes `Borrowed`s with drawers of its own, reads the drawer while one lives and after it ends, throws an exception of its own while one lives, and borrows a tool the drawer has none of. It also tries two lines of its own that copy a `Borrowed`, which must not compile.
nextSteps: Give the class two private members: a reference to the drawer and the tool's name, set in the initialiser list.
In the constructor, throw before anything changes when the drawer has none of the tool; then take one out.
Write the destructor, which puts one back.
Forbid copies with the two = delete lines the lesson shows.
hints: A constructor that throws leaves no object, so no destructor runs for it. Whatever it took before the throw is never put back.
count or find on the map tells whether the tool is there at all, without adding it; [] on a missing key adds it with 0. A reference member gets its value in the initialiser list.

The shape is `Borrowed(std::map<std::string, int>& from, const std::string& name) : drawer(from), tool(name) { if (drawer.count(tool) == 0 || drawer.at(tool) <= 0) { throw std::runtime_error("no " + tool + " left"); } drawer.at(tool) -= 1; }`, `~Borrowed() { drawer[tool] += 1; }`, and `Borrowed(const Borrowed&) = delete; Borrowed& operator=(const Borrowed&) = delete;`.

tasks.title: Fit parts with the loupe
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, write a function called `fitWithLoupe` that takes the drawer as a reference to a `std::map<std::string, int>`, a repair as a reference to a `Repair`, and the parts as a reference to a `const std::vector<std::string>`, and gives back an `int`. It borrows the `"loupe"` from the drawer with a `Borrowed`, holds it while it fits each part to the repair with `fitPart`, in order, and gives back how many parts it fitted. When a part does not fit, or there is no loupe, the exception goes on to the caller, and the loupe is back in the drawer whatever happened.

Check builds this task with a `Borrowed` of its own and a `fitPart` of its own, which notes whether the loupe was held at each part. It calls `fitWithLoupe` with drawers and parts of its own, reads the drawer afterwards, and catches what comes out.
nextSteps: Make a named Borrowed of the loupe on the first line.
Fit each part with fitPart, and count the parts fitted.
Put no try in it: the Borrowed puts the loupe back on every way out.
hints: A Borrowed is a local: its destructor runs at the closing } and when an exception leaves the function. That is all the cleanup this function needs.
Borrowed(drawer, "loupe"); with no name ends at the end of its own line, and new Borrowed(...) never ends at all. Neither holds the loupe while the parts are fitted.
The shape is `Borrowed loupe(drawer, "loupe"); int fitted = 0; for (const std::string& part : parts) { fitPart(repair, part); fitted = fitted + 1; } return fitted;`.
